summary: This document introduces the YANG module iana-dns-class-rr-type, which holds derived types reflecting two IANA registries: DNS CLASSes and Resource Record TYPEs. They are the minimum basis for future DNS data modeling.

eli5.summary: DNS records come in many kinds, each with a number. This document makes a list of those kinds in a form that other configuration descriptions can reuse.

subtitle: Two DNS registries, DNS CLASSes and RR TYPEs, translated into reusable YANG types.

tldr.problem: Management tools that use YANG with NETCONF or RESTCONF need a shared way to name DNS classes and resource record types, or every DNS data model must invent its own.
tldr.mechanism: The YANG module iana-dns-class-rr-type defines the types dns-class and rr-type. Each accepts either a 16-bit number or a mnemonic name taken from the matching IANA registry, and IANA keeps the module in step with those registries.
tldr.outcome: Future DNS data models can import these two types as a common starting point. The document introduces no new protocol, and its security impact is nil on its own.

today: RFC 9108 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA is directed to keep the module in step with the two registries it reflects.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs YANG Types
sections.content:
YANG is a language for modeling configuration and state data, management operations and notifications. Together with management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF it could be used for DNS operations: configuring authoritative servers, resolvers and zone data.

The RFC argues that the real benefit comes only from a unified data model supported by several DNS implementations. Operators could then run several server implementations in parallel with one management interface, and moving to another implementation would become easier. The authors expect building such models to be lengthy and to need cooperation from the major DNS vendors.

Any such model will need the parameters and enumerations in IANA registries. This RFC translates two fundamental ones into YANG, a step it calls straightforward and relatively uncontroversial.
sections.eli5: If every toy company labelled its toy boxes differently, sorting them would be a mess. This document gives everyone the same labels for DNS record kinds.

sections.title: The Module and Its Types
sections.content:
The module is named iana-dns-class-rr-type. At the time of writing, the IANA Domain Name System (DNS) Parameters page held thirteen registries, and the module covers only two: DNS CLASSes and Resource Record (RR) TYPEs. The RFC expects the other registries to be reflected in future modules as needed.

Each registry becomes a YANG enumeration, dns-class-name and rr-type-name. An entry such as IN carries its value (1), a description and a reference (RFC 1035).

The types people actually use are dns-class and rr-type. Each is a union of a uint16 and the matching enumeration. This follows RFC 3597, which allows a class or type to be written by its decimal number, for example CLASS1 for IN or TYPE28 for AAAA.

Unassigned and reserved values are left out of the enumerations, so they can only be given as decimal numbers.
sections.eli5: A type can be written as a name or as a number, like calling a friend by name or by their locker number. Values nobody has been given yet only have numbers.

sections.title: How IANA Keeps the Module Current
sections.content:
IANA created the initial module by running the XSLT stylesheet in the RFC's appendix against the XML version of the DNS Parameters registry. The latest module is available from the YANG Parameters registry.

When a class or RR type is added to its registry, a new enum statement SHALL be added to the module. Its name is the mnemonic name, and its substatements are set as follows.

  • value: the decimal value from the registry.
  • status: included only if the registration is deprecated or obsoleted, mapping to the YANG statuses deprecated and obsolete.
  • description: the full class name or the meaning of the type, if any.
  • reference: the references from the registry.

Unassigned or reserved values SHALL NOT be included, and each update adds a new revision statement before the existing ones. Changes must be made in the registries, never directly in the module, and IANA added notes saying so to the registries and to the module's entry.

The module has the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:iana-dns-class-rr-type and the prefix dnsct.
sections.eli5: When a new kind of DNS record is added to the official list, IANA must add it to the YANG copy too. Nobody may edit the copy by hand.

sections.title: The XSLT Stylesheet
sections.content:
Appendix A holds an XSLT 1.0 stylesheet that is meant for IANA to generate the first version of the module. It is applied to the XML version of the DNS Parameters registry, for example with xsltproc iana-dns-class-rr-type.xsl dns-parameters.xml.

The stylesheet writes the module header, then an enum for each record of the two registries. It skips unassigned and reserved entries, and marks an entry status obsolete when its description contains the word OBSOLETE. For classes, the name comes from the text in parentheses in the description, when there is any.
sections.eli5: The stylesheet is a recipe that turns the official list into the YANG version automatically, so no one has to copy it by hand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC translates two IANA registries into YANG data types and introduces no technology or protocol. The definitions themselves have no security impact on the Internet, but their use in concrete YANG modules might.

The security considerations in the YANG specification, RFC 7950, apply to this document as well.
sections.eli5: This is only a list of names, so it cannot cause harm by itself. Care is needed only when the list is used in real tools.
